content: Erythroderma is a severe and widespread skin condition characterized by redness and scaling that affects the entire skin surface, covering 100% of the body. It is also referred to as erythrodermatitis, generalized exfoliative dermatitis, or red man syndrome. In some cases, small areas of normal skin may still be present amidst the affected regions. Erythroderma can result from a variety of underlying skin disorders, including psoriasis, contact dermatitis, adverse drug reactions, and mycosis fungoides, which is a type of cutaneous lymphoma. Identifying the underlying cause is critical and typically requires a thorough evaluation by a dermatologist. Diagnostic methods often include a skin biopsy, blood smear analysis by a pathologist, and patch testing if the skin eruption can be temporarily resolved. Certain medications are known to induce erythroderma. These include, but are not limited to, the following drugs: Amobarbital sodium Amoxicillin Amifostine Aminophylline Aminosalicylic acid Alitretinoin Aztreonam Boceprevir Chlorpropamide Doxycycline Dapsone Flurbiprofen Ibritumomab tiuxetan Lincomycin Hydrochloride Nizatidine Oxaprozin Oxytetracycline Pembrolizumab Piroxicam Sodium aurothiomalate Sorafenib Sulfasalazine Sirolimus Tiagabine Trimethadione The management and treatment of erythroderma depend entirely on addressing the underlying cause.
